title: Measuring Layer-wise Intrinsic Dimensionality of FFNs in LLMs via PCA
claim: A characteristic middle-layer dip in reconstruction fidelity recurs across very different calibration corpora, so the pattern is robust to data choice.
layout: 2x3 grid of line plots, shared axes, one colorbar on right
description: Six small line-plot panels in a 2x3 grid share the same axes. Each panel is titled with a calibration corpus: SlimPajama, MMLU, ARC-C, HellaSwag, WikiText, and Chinese SkyPile. The x-axis is layer index (0-35). The y-axis is cosine similarity between the activation and its PCA reconstruction (about 0.6 to 1.0). Each panel has nine curves, one per width fraction from 10% to 90%. A vertical colorbar on the right maps the fractions from orange-red (10%) to blue (90%). A red dashed horizontal line near 0.99 marks the threshold. The low-width curves dip deeply in the middle layers and rise at the edges, forming a U shape. The high-width curves are flat near 1.0. The panels look nearly identical, and the eye goes first to the repeated dip in the orange curves.
caption: Calibration robustness on Qwen3-8B. Per-layer cosine similarity between hl and its rank-d PCA reconstruction at width fractions d/Dl ∈{10%, 20%, . . . , 90%}, measured on six 100K- token calibration corpora: five English (SlimPajama, MMLU, ARC-C, HellaSwag, WikiText) and Chinese SkyPile. Red dashed line marks the θ = 0.99 threshold. All six panels show the same dip at middle layers when d/Dl is small, indicating that more principal directions are required to faithfully reconstruct middle-layer activations. Pairwise per-layer Pearson r on the extracted dθ,l/Dl profiles: five English corpora min 0.953, mean 0.975; English ↔Chinese min 0.941, mean 0.973; all 15 pairs ≥0.941, with the minimum occurring between Chinese SkyPile and HellaSwag.
abstract: Modern large language models (LLMs) keep the feed-forward network (FFN) intermediate width identical across every layer, a convention inherited from the original Transformer. Yet mechanistic work suggests layers at different depths do qualitatively different work, raising a natural question: are their capacity demands also non-uniform, and if so, can a fixed parameter budget be allocated more wisely than uniformly? To probe this, we apply principal component analysis (PCA) to the input of each FFN down-projection and measure, for every layer, its intrinsic dimensionality as the smallest number of principal components needed to reconstruct the activation up to a fixed cosine similarity. Scanning 58 open-weight LLMs spanning 14 families and 70M to 72B parameters, we find a recurring middle-heavy profile in which middle layers carry higher intrinsic dimensionality than edge layers; the profile is robust to the calibration corpus, even across English and Chinese, and is largely preserved through post-training fine-tuning. As a direct test that this signal is structurally meaningful, we use it to guide width pruning in a knowledge-distilled student under a matched parameter budget: the PCA-guided allocation outperforms the uniform-width convention by +2.3 points on Qwen3-8B and +2.5 on Qwen2.5-3B, while lower-dispersion teachers show smaller gaps (+0.9 on Gemma-3-4B, +0.5 on LLaMA-3-8B), and a budget-matched inverted control does worst on all four teachers. Across these four teachers, the size of the gap tracks how unevenly the teacher's intrinsic dimensionality is distributed across layers (a single-number summary we call $Ï_{99}$), and the advantage persists through downstream supervised fine-tuning. Code is available at https://github.com/naver-ai/lidf.
